title: Rekey or Replace Your Locks?

category.name: Locksmith
category.description: Locks, keys and home security: when rekeying is enough, when hardware has to be replaced, and how to avoid the locksmith scams that follow a lockout.
category.seoDescription: Rekeying versus replacement explained: costs, when each makes sense, what a locksmith should charge, and how to spot an unlicensed operator.

audience: New homeowners and anyone who has lost a key, ended a tenancy or inherited unknown keys.

internalLinks.label: Questions to ask before hiring a home service professional

imageAlt: Illustration of a key with a security shield and a coin
seoTitle: Rekey or Replace Your Locks? Costs and When to Do Each
seoDescription: Rekeying changes the pins, replacement changes the hardware. Which one you need after moving house, losing a key or upgrading security — and what each costs.
excerpt: Rekeying is cheaper, faster and just as secure for most homes. Replacement is for hardware that is failing, outdated or not worth keeping — and the difference matters.
seoSummary: Comparison of rekeying and lock replacement with cost, security and scenario guidance.
author: Safe Home Network Editorial
visual: Flat vector medallion: a brass key with a shield chip, a coin chip and a check chip on a cream background.

paras: Rekeying and replacing are often treated as the same job. They are not. Rekeying changes the pins inside an existing lock so the old key no longer works; replacement changes the whole lock body, handles, and sometimes the door preparation.
For most homeowners who simply need to know that no one else has a key, rekeying is the right answer and costs a fraction of replacement.

head: Rekey
Replace
rows: The entire lock and handle set
Longer, especially if the door needs modification
Identical to a new lock of the same grade
Better only if the new hardware is a higher grade
Lost keys, new home, tenant turnover

sections.h2: Rekey when the hardware is fine
bullets: You have just moved in and do not know who else has a key.
A key was lost or stolen, or a roommate or tenant has moved out.
You want every exterior door on one key instead of a ring of five.
The locks work smoothly and are a reasonable grade.
You have bought a home with a builder-grade lock that still functions well.
paras: Rekeying also lets a locksmith key all exterior doors alike — one key for the front, back and side — which is a genuine convenience and often costs little more than rekeying a single cylinder.

sections.h2: Replace when the hardware is the problem
bullets: The lock is loose, wobbly or has a cylinder that turns without engaging.
The key sticks, or the lock must be jiggled to work — worn pins or a damaged cylinder.
The door has settled and the lock no longer aligns with the strike.
The lock is a low-grade builder model on an entry door and you want a deadbolt with a proper ANSI grade.
You want a smart lock or a keypad, which replaces the hardware by definition.
There is visible damage from a break-in attempt or forced entry.

paras: Deadbolts are graded by ANSI: Grade 3 is builder-grade, Grade 2 is a solid residential step up, Grade 1 is the strongest commonly available. The other half of the equation is installation: a Grade 1 deadbolt held by half-inch screws into a soft frame is weaker than a Grade 2 with a reinforced strike and long screws into the stud.
If you upgrade one thing, upgrade the strike plate and the screws holding it. It is cheap and it addresses the most common way a door is defeated.
sections.note: Never hide a spare key outside. Leave one with a trusted neighbor or use a keypad; a fake rock is the first place anyone looks.

sections.h2: What a locksmith should cost, and what should worry you
paras: A rekey is usually a service call plus a per-cylinder charge; a replacement adds hardware cost. Ask for the total before work starts, including the service call, and confirm whether the price is per lock or per visit.

Be careful with the companies that dominate emergency-lockout search results. Warning signs: no local address, a call center that will not quote a price, a technician who arrives without identification, and a bill far above the quoted amount once the door is open. Look up the business licence and ask for the total in writing before anyone touches the lock.

sections.h2: After a break-in or a lost key
ordered: Rekey every exterior lock, not just the one that was used.
Check the door frame and strike for damage — a kicked door often damages the frame, not the lock.
Consider a reinforced strike and longer screws while the locksmith is there.
If the door itself is damaged, read our front door replacement guide before authorising a full replacement.
Update any insurance records and photographs of the property.

faqs.q: Is rekeying as secure as replacing?
faqs.a: Yes, if the existing hardware is in good condition and of a decent grade. Rekeying gives you a brand-new key series; it does not improve the physical strength of the lock.
Typically a service call plus a modest charge per cylinder. It is considerably cheaper than replacing locks, which adds hardware cost on top of labour.
On standard cylindrical locksets, yes, with a rekey kit and some patience. On high-security or smart locks, and on any lock you rely on for security, a professional is the safer choice.

faqs.q: Should I change the locks when I move into a rental?
faqs.a: Ask the landlord first — tenants usually cannot change locks without permission. Many jurisdictions require the landlord to rekey between tenancies; check your lease and local rules.
